title: Why Recruiters Skip Your CV in Seconds (39,184 CVs Analysed)
description:
Why Recruiters Skip Your CV in Seconds (39,184 CVs Analysed)

FREE GUIDE:
My free CV Guide has the CV template plus the exact ChatGPT prompt series for tailoring it to any job description.
https://offeraccelerator.co.uk/join-free-training-organic?source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=why-recruiters-skip-your-cv


CONNECT WITH ME
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/olivercordingley
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/o.cordingley


WATCH NEXT:
ATS Isn't Rejecting Your CV. This Is. (3 Real Filters)
https://youtu.be/lhxQi9nupHU?si=3GCqLtMiNlwBR8pY

A study of 39,184 CVs compared which ones led to an interview and which ones were ignored. This video walks through what that research actually measured, the CV findings that change your interview rate, and what happens in the 6 to 10 seconds a recruiter spends on your CV on the first pass, which is a separate thing the study never tracked.

If your CV is getting rejected and you have been rewriting it for every application without getting interviews, this is the evidence base to work from.


What you'll learn in this video:
- What the 39,184 CV study measured, its 3 limits, and the claims it does not support
- Why tailoring doubled the interview rate, 4.23% against 2.07%
- Why the one page CV rule is dead, 2 pages interviewed at 7.40% against 5.01%
- The F shaped scan pattern and the 3 things that pull a recruiter's eye in the first 6 to 10 seconds
- Why an ATS score is a number no employer ever sees, and what knockout questions really filter


VIDEO CHAPTERS:
0:00 Why recruiters skip a CV in seconds
0:40 The source, the sample, and the method
2:30 What the study never measured
0:54 Tailoring, 4.23% against 2.07%
1:08 A hard number in your summary
1:24 CV length and bullet depth
1:52 Averages are not rules, and the 2 to 4 year trough
3:11 The 6 to 10 second scan and the F pattern
3:49 The 3 things that pull a recruiter's eye
4:36 The ATS myth and knockout questions
5:46 One role, one CV, and visible proof
6:51 The before and after bullet rewrite
8:13 The 5 point second look check


Run the 5 point check on your own CV, and use my template and prompts to fix what it turns up.

ABOUT ME:
I dropped out of university at 19 to build recruitment software and ATS systems used by hiring teams. For years I spoke to hundreds of hiring managers and recruiters every day, learning exactly how candidates get filtered, shortlisted, and hired from the inside. I started coaching friends through their job search using what I'd seen, then raised investment, built a software company, and hired my own team. I've seen hiring from every angle.

Today I help job seekers land offers faster using a proven 3-step system. I've coached hundreds of candidates into roles at firms like JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, EY, and PwC and many more.

So, there was 39,184 real CVs and they compared on whether they, you know, led it to an interview or they just got rejected. Now, the biggest single difference was tailoring. So, CVs that got tailored to the job interviewed at 4.23%. The ones that weren't came in at 2.07%. Now, that is almost double the interview rate and nothing comes close to that biggest change. Now, secondly, a hard number in the summary section. So, in the report, summaries carrying some sort of numerical figure like dollar, pound, percentages, they amounted to interviews at 6.97% whereas summaries with no digits in there, they only interviewed at 4.78%. Now, the third factor was the length of the CV and this is the one that sort of annoys the most people. So, two pages or more interviewed at 7.4%. Whereas one page it only came in at 5%. That's 48% better for the longer CV. So, the one page rule is pretty much dead for most people nowadays. Now, the fourth finding was then the bullet point depth. So, CVs with one to five bullets in total interviewed at I think it was about 5% and CVs with 21 to 30 bullet points, they came in at 7.92%. Now, those are averages across a very mixed pool and averages obviously aren't rules. So, the length-finding, it does have some exceptions sort of sitting alongside it because candidates with roughly sort of like 3 to 10 years of experience actually did better with one-pagers in the report. So, the study breaks interview rates down by sort of like the years of experience, and it comes out more like like looking like a U-shape. So, 20 or more years sort of peaks at 9.2% interview rate. Now, the bottom of that curve, which is the hardest band to basically get an interview, is people with two to four years of experience at only 3%. So, you could apply the same advice to everybody else, but there's a very different ceiling depending on where you are in your career. So, that's what sort of like the data says with this report, but that study never really timed a recruiter, and it never really tracked anybody's eyes on the CV. So, here's the part it can't see, which is what actually happens when a human opens it and then looks at your CV. So, that's what the data says based on all the CVs and where they actually ended up getting interviews or not, but the study does kind of ignore sort of like the human element of hiring, and people still forget that humans are an integral part of the recruitment process even in 2026. So, once you pass the sort of application form, your CV will sit in a queue, and a real recruiter and a real human will open it if you pass the knockout questions. And this is completely contrary to belief about, you know, ATS automatically rejecting you, cuz that's not how it works. Now, on a first pass, they're sort of giving it somewhere between 6 to 10 seconds. Now, that's quite a typical range. There's not some sort of stopwatch, and they're timed exactly, but roughly speaking, it's in that time range. Now, the way that hiring managers, recruiters, talent acquisition team members, the way that they look at a CV is actually also been researched as well with eye-tracking software. And it basically boils down to this. People scan CVs in a capital F-shape. So, what they do is they scan across the top of the page, then down the left, and then sort of picking up a few job titles and companies along that list. Now, what this means is is that the top third gets the most attention, and the left side gets read more than the right-hand side. And the bottom of the page, too, it barely sort of gets looked at. Now, there are three things that pull the eye in into that scan when someone is looking at your CV. So, the first is hard numbers because a figure is concrete, it makes them stop and it stands out visibly. The second element is then recognizable names. So, these are companies, tools, certifications that they would be familiar with and they would know. And then finally, the language of the job description itself because the recruiter or the hiring manager that has their set requirements in their head, they're matching words subconsciously and it's registering when you look at your CV. So, with the study with the eye-tracking software and the 39,000 CV review, and you'll notice that both of those reports actually shared the same three things. And it basically shares that what is actually rewarded in a CV or not. So, you've got the numbers, you've got the tailored language, and you've also got the layout in accommodating with the F-scan. So, the study found the pattern in the outcomes and the scan is one of the explanations for why those things actually matter. Now, the part that most candidates get wrong and it, you know, this kind of cost them real interviews is they believe that ATS reads their CV, scores it against keywords, and then rejects them if the score is too low. But, there's no universal ATS score that decides every application. Some application forms have knockout questions and they basically disqualify you before a human ever opens your CV. Other systems, they pass, organize, search, or rank the applications for the recruiters. Then a human opens a CV and decides whether enough, you know, to take you further into an interview. Now, the real automated filter is the knockout questions, not some sort of ATS score. So, those are binary yes or no items on the application form. So, when you make an application and one of those answers is wrong based on your CV, then you will be filtered out before anybody opens your CV. So, there are three separate stages and people sort of collapse them into one. So, the form knocks you out, the system then passes and ranks you, and then a human scans it. So, that's how a CV is processed. And that is why a tool selling you an ATS score is selling you a number that no employer ever sees. It's not even relevant to the recruitment space. There is no such thing as an ATS score. So, here's how as a candidate I would use all of this information to my advantage. So, the first thing is pick one target role and build one CV for it. So, don't go and create 20 almost identical versions aimed at 20 different job titles because the moment you spread across 20 titles, you just look like everybody else trying to apply and you're not being consistent and then you can't then defend yourself in an interview. Then, the second thing is you need to position it. So, the job title at the top of your CV should match the title on the advert. Now, if you don't feel comfortable writing that title, that's probably a sign that you're applying to the wrong role anyway. Then, you need to make your proof visible and visible means in that top third and down the left-hand side. So, a number buried in the last bullet of page two, it you know, it might as well not exist. It's not going to be seen. And also like if you're in that two to four year experience band, you need to be honest with yourself about what the CV can do because your CV is being compared, it's getting read next to people with probably two to three times your experience. So, making it better raises a ceiling that was kind of low to start with, which is why candidates that I work with spend less time on the CV than they actually expect to and far more on which roles they should go after and then who they know inside those companies. So, let me show you what that looks like on sort of like, you know, a real example. So, say the job advert asked for experience with stakeholder management across, you know, cross-functional teams and your bullet currently reads led the quarterly project review with engineering, marketing and operations teams. That is a decent bullet, but it's just not written in their words. So, the recruiter has to translate it and in that six-second scan, they probably won't bother. So, you rewrite it as something like this. Led quarterly stakeholder management across cross-functional teams in engineering, marketing and operations cutting review time by 30%. So, that is the exact same work and experience and you've matched their language and you've added the number that catches the eye and then you move that bullet into the top of that role so that it lands in that zone that actually gets scanned. Now, if you're not sure about where your CV stands at the moment, here's sort of like a second look check. So, I'm going to talk you through five things and every one of them is something the evidence actually supports. So, the first thing is you need to pull up the last job description you applied to and see if you can find five phrases from that advert inside your CV, just in your own true sentences. The second thing is then look at the job title at the top of your CV and ask whether it's the title on the advert or like maybe one step under it. Now, the third thing is then find the top third of your page one on the CV and check there's at least one hard number and one recognizable name sitting in it. Now, the fourth thing is then count those bullets in your most recent role. If there are sort of like two or three then you're under the average. What you want is sort of that three to five range and and everyone needs at least a result in it. And then the fifth and final thing is then go back to the application form questions, not the CV, and then work out whether you actually met every hard requirement. And that's the one stage that could automatically reject you. So, the real lesson from that 39,000 plus CV study isn't some sort of magic template or a fake ATS score, is making sure that your CV survives all three of those stages that I've just walked you through. So, if you want the template and the exact prompt series that I use to do all of that against the job description, my free CV guide is linked in the description. It's got the CV template itself plus the prompts for tailoring it to any advert. So, go and grab that and then run the five-point check before you send the next one.
